paragraphs: Bayesian models can describe human perceptual behavior very well, but a good behavioral fit does not necessarily reveal a unique internal explanation. Different combinations of prior expectations, sensory likelihoods, and loss functions can produce indistinguishable observations. The paper studies identifiability: whether the available evidence can distinguish those underlying components.

The authors propose a framework for systematically testing identifiability across a substantial class of Bayesian observer models. This makes the question part of experimental design. Instead of interpreting a fitted internal representation solely through its agreement with behavior, researchers can examine whether their experiment separates it from alternative representations.

Two case studies illustrate the framework. For time interval estimation, the analysis identifies experimental designs that better resolve the ambiguity between model components. For speed perception with a slow-speed prior, the reconstructed representations are found to be fairly robust. Together, these findings show how identifiability analysis can both guide better experiments and strengthen confidence in particular interpretations, depending on the task and model.
neurips-2014-a-framework-for-testing-ide.tldr: A framework tests whether Bayesian perception models uniquely identify internal representations and helps design experiments that resolve ambiguities.

paragraphs: Topic models describe documents through recurring themes, but models such as LDA assume that words are independent within a topic. The Admixture of Poisson MRFs model, or APM, explicitly represents dependencies between words within each theme. This paper addresses the computational expense of that richer representation and how to evaluate whether its dependencies capture meaning.

APM needs a number of parameters that grows quadratically with vocabulary size. Earlier results were limited to vocabularies of 200 words. The authors develop a parallel training algorithm that alternates Newton-like updates and can handle 10,000 words. This is presented as a substantial step toward larger datasets, rather than a complete solution to scaling.

The paper also introduces an evaluation measure based on human judgments of how strongly one word brings another to mind. That measure directly connects learned word relationships to semantic associations. Quantitative and qualitative results on the BNC corpus favor APM over previous topic models for identifying meaningful dependencies, providing stronger evidence for the model's usefulness than the earlier tentative evaluations.
neurips-2014-capturing-semantically-mean.tldr: Faster training and a human-association evaluation strengthen APM's case for modeling meaningful word dependencies within topics.

paragraphs: The paper studies recovery of signals when only incomplete linear measurements are available. It assumes the signals follow a Gaussian mixture model whose precision matrices are sparse. The difficult feature of the setting is that the mixture model is itself unknown: there are neither known mixture parameters nor fully observed training signals to establish them beforehand.

The authors develop a hierarchical Bayesian method that learns the mixture model and reconstructs the signals together. A Bayesian shrinkage prior encourages sparse precision matrices, incorporating the assumed structure into estimation. Joint inference allows the incomplete measurements to inform both the recovered signals and the statistical model used to recover them.

The theory connects reconstruction error to three features of the problem: how many signals have measurements, how sparse the precision matrices are, and how incomplete the measurements are. Experiments cover imagery and video using both simulated measurements and measurements acquired by hardware. The reported improvements over leading methods support the value of learning this structured signal model directly from incomplete observations.
neurips-2014-compressive-sensing-of-sign.tldr: A hierarchical Bayesian method jointly learns a structured Gaussian mixture and reconstructs signals using only incomplete measurements.

paragraphs: Recommendation systems benefit from information about users' preferences, creating a tension between prediction accuracy and willingness to disclose those preferences. This paper considers a population with two privacy expectations: a small group openly shares its preferences, while a much larger group requires privacy guarantees. This separation gives the authors a way to study how different sources of information contribute.

The first result concerns what can be achieved using public information alone. Theoretical analysis and empirical evidence show that a moderate number of public users can suffice for reasonable recommendation accuracy without accessing private users' information. The stated result is about obtaining useful accuracy, rather than eliminating every accuracy cost associated with privacy.

The authors then introduce a privacy concept that permits extracting relational information from private users while preserving what they call first order deniability. They demonstrate gains from this controlled access to preferences. Together, the results examine both the usefulness of openly shared data and the additional benefit available under a more selective form of private information access.
neurips-2014-controlling-privacy-in-reco.tldr: A two-tier privacy framework studies useful recommendations from public users and further gains from controlled access to private preferences.

paragraphs: Traditional convolutional networks process an image through a fixed sequence of layers without feedback from higher layers to lower ones. This paper introduces dasNet, a network whose feedback connections can alter the sensitivities of convolutional filters during classification. Its internal processing can therefore adapt as it examines an input.

The central mechanism is sequential attention within the network. Across successive processing steps, feedback allows dasNet to focus selectively on some of its filters. This makes classification an iterative process in which internal emphasis can change, rather than relying entirely on the responses produced by one fixed forward evaluation.

The feedback behavior is trained using direct policy search with scalable natural evolution strategies, operating in a parameter space with about a million dimensions. On CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 without dataset augmentation, dasNet surpasses the previous state-of-the-art model reported in the abstract. These results support the usefulness of learned feedback and repeated internal attention in the evaluated classification setting; the architectural contribution is the ability to adjust filter sensitivity during evaluation.
neurips-2014-deep-networks-with-internal.tldr: DasNet learns feedback that adjusts convolutional filter sensitivities during iterative classification, improving results on unaugmented CIFAR datasets.

paragraphs: Some datasets are modeled as several classes, each associated with a subspace, with those subspaces assumed to be independent. Reducing the number of dimensions can interfere with that structure. This paper asks how to compress such data while preserving the independence that makes the original model useful.

The central theoretical result says that 2K projection vectors are sufficient for preserving independence in K-class data sampled from a union of independent subspaces. This is a sufficiency statement under the stated structural assumption; it does not say that every projection works or that 2K is always the smallest possible number. The authors use this result to design a dimensionality reduction algorithm with a structure-preservation guarantee for a given dataset.

Experiments on synthetic and real data support the theoretical analysis, with the authors reporting state-of-the-art results against popular dimensionality reduction techniques. The contribution connects a specific geometric property to the design of the projection itself. It makes preservation of the assumed class subspaces an explicit objective of compression.
neurips-2014-dimensionality-reduction-wi.tldr: The paper uses a sufficient 2K-projection result to reduce dimensions while preserving independent subspace structure in K-class data.

paragraphs: The paper studies sequential prediction games in which errors are measured by squared distance. It covers both ordinary squared Euclidean distance and squared Mahalanobis distance, which allows a more general weighting of errors. The goal is to derive strategies that are optimal against worst-case play within the specified games.

The analysis treats two geometries for the prediction and action spaces: the simplex and the Euclidean ball. The simplex setting is associated with the Brier game, while the ball setting is related to Gaussian density estimation. For both, the authors show that the value of every remaining sub-game can be expressed as a quadratic function of a simple statistic summarizing the state.

An explicit recurrence efficiently computes the coefficients of that quadratic function. From this representation, the paper obtains a deterministic minimax strategy and a randomized maximin strategy, each linear in the same statistic. The result turns the underlying sequential optimization into a compact calculation, providing both optimal game strategies and an efficient way to evaluate them for these settings.
neurips-2014-efficient-minimax-strategie.tldr: Square-loss prediction games on the simplex and Euclidean ball admit efficiently computable optimal strategies based on a simple state statistic.

paragraphs: The paper addresses recovery of matrices that must satisfy a specified structure while also having low rank. It represents the structure through a linear map and encourages low rank with nuclear norm regularization. The computational challenge is to make this combination practical without expensive operations dominating each optimization step.

The authors reformulate the problem so that a generalized conditional gradient method can solve it. Their approach avoids a full singular value decomposition, augmented Lagrangian techniques, and solving linear systems at every iteration. These choices matter because they reduce the cost of individual updates, which is the stated source of the method's practical improvement.

Numerical experiments evaluate the approach on stochastic system realization and spectral compressed sensing. The reported results show substantially shorter running times than state-of-the-art competitors while still recovering low-rank solutions effectively. The contribution therefore joins a different optimization formulation with evidence that cheaper iterations can translate into useful overall speed gains on structured matrix recovery problems.
neurips-2014-efficient-structured-matrix.tldr: A generalized conditional gradient formulation reduces iteration costs and speeds up structured low-rank matrix recovery in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Large convolutional networks can recognize objects accurately, but evaluating each image requires substantial arithmetic. This creates deployment difficulties both on smartphones and in systems processing images at Internet scale. The paper focuses on reducing the computation needed at test time, when an already trained model is used to make predictions.

The authors identify convolution operations in the lower layers as the dominant computational expense. They exploit redundancy among convolutional filters to construct approximations that require less computation. The key idea is that the filters' existing linear structure offers opportunities to simplify evaluation while retaining much of the original model's predictive behavior.

Experiments with large state-of-the-art models demonstrate a twofold speedup for convolutional layers on both CPUs and GPUs, with accuracy remaining within 1% of the original model. That speedup applies to the convolutional layers measured in the study. The findings show a practical tradeoff: approximating redundant filter computations can substantially reduce an expensive part of inference while keeping the reported accuracy close to its original level.
neurips-2014-exploiting-linear-structure.tldr: Approximating redundant convolutional filters yields reported twofold layer speedups on CPUs and GPUs while keeping accuracy within 1%.

paragraphs: Many statistical quantities summarize entire probability densities rather than individual observations. This paper analyzes a plug-in estimator for a broad class of such quantities, including entropy, divergence, mutual information, and conditional versions. The plug-in approach estimates the relevant densities and uses those estimates to calculate the desired integral functional.

The theoretical setting assumes continuous densities on a d-dimensional unit cube that belong to a beta-Hölder smoothness class. Within this setting, the authors establish a convergence result whose stated rate depends on both smoothness and dimension. These assumptions connect the estimator's behavior to the regularity and dimensionality of the underlying distributions.

The paper also proves an exponential concentration inequality around the estimator's mean. This addresses how strongly individual estimates can fluctuate, adding information beyond a bound on average estimation error alone. The authors illustrate the bounds for conditional Rényi mutual information. The contribution is thus a shared theoretical treatment of many density-based quantities, with particular attention to probabilistic control of deviations as well as convergence.
neurips-2014-exponential-concentration-o.tldr: A plug-in estimator for density-based quantities receives convergence and exponential concentration guarantees under stated support and smoothness assumptions.

paragraphs: Some resource-allocation problems aim to discover an unusually large observation rather than obtain a high average reward. The paper studies this objective when resources must be assigned sequentially among several sources and feedback is limited. Network intrusion detection is one motivating example in which extreme outputs can be the quantities of interest.

Conventional bandit objectives often compare a learner with the source having the best mean reward. Here, the authors introduce extreme regret, which compares performance with an oracle policy that selects the source with the heaviest tail. This changes the reference for success: the relevant source is characterized by its potential for extreme outcomes rather than its average output.

The paper proposes ExtremeHunter, analyzes the algorithm, and evaluates it on synthetic and real-world experiments. Its central contribution is to organize sequential exploration around extreme-value discovery. The framework provides a way to assess whether limited sampling resources are being directed effectively when rare, large observations matter more to the task than consistently favorable ordinary observations.
neurips-2014-extreme-bandits-e70c395b8c.tldr: ExtremeHunter studies sequential resource allocation for discovering extreme observations using regret relative to a heaviest-tail oracle.

paragraphs: Transfer learning uses a well-supplied source task to help a related target task with little labeled data. The paper examines cases where the domains differ more broadly than standard transfer assumptions allow. In particular, the target may contain values outside the source distribution's support, and the relationships between observations and labels may also change.

The authors discuss restrictions in covariate-shift and target-shift approaches, including assumptions that the source covers the target's relevant support. They consider a more flexible setting with limited target labels and smooth changes across distributions. Their method transforms both observations X and labels Y through location-scale shifts, allowing changes in where values lie and how they are scaled.

Transforming both sides of the supervised problem gives the method flexibility to handle changes in support as well as changes in the model. The authors report better results on synthetic and real-world data with these transformations. The findings support this particular approach to broader domain differences, while its stated mechanism remains the use of location-scale transformations.
neurips-2014-flexible-transfer-learning-.tldr: Location-scale transformations of both observations and labels enable transfer learning when domain support and model relationships change.

paragraphs: Missing entries can make a statistical or causal question impossible to answer from the observed data, but the answer depends on how missingness occurs. This paper assumes a model of that process and asks which queries remain recoverable. It covers conditional probabilities, joint probabilities, and causal effects expressed through interventions.

The authors derive more general graphical conditions for recovering these queries. A central finding is that a causal effect may be recoverable even when individual factors in an expression identifying that effect are not. Thus, inspecting the recoverability of every factor separately can miss cases in which the causal query as a whole can still be obtained.

The analysis includes conditions for recovering causal effects when the outcome and its missingness mechanism are not separated by the graph's d-separation criterion. The authors also apply their results to attrition, characterizing recovery of causal effects when observations are lost through that process. The contribution provides query-specific reasoning about missing data, with conclusions tied to the supplied model of missingness.
neurips-2014-graphical-models-for-recove.tldr: Graphical conditions identify recoverable statistical and causal queries under missingness, including some effects whose identifying factors are unrecoverable.

paragraphs: Recognizing a scene means identifying the broader visual setting, which can also provide context for recognizing objects. The paper observes that progress in scene recognition had not matched progress in object recognition. It suggests that features learned from object-focused ImageNet data may be insufficiently suited to scene tasks, motivating a dataset centered on scenes.

The authors introduce Places, containing more than seven million labeled scene pictures. They also propose ways to compare the density and diversity of image datasets. Under these comparisons, Places has density comparable to other scene datasets while offering greater diversity. This evaluates the collection along dimensions beyond its raw image count.

Using Places to train convolutional networks, the authors learn features that establish new state-of-the-art results on several scene-focused datasets. Visualizations of layer responses also reveal differences between the internal representations of object-focused and scene-focused networks. The results connect the choice of training images to both recognition performance and the kinds of representations learned inside a network.
neurips-2014-learning-deep-features-for-.tldr: Places supplies over seven million labeled scene images and enables scene-trained CNN features with leading reported recognition results.

paragraphs: The paper studies how much memory is needed to approximate a matrix when its rows arrive one at a time in arbitrary order. After seeing the stream, an algorithm must output a compact matrix with k rows. The subspace represented by that output must approximate the original matrix nearly as well as the best rank-k approximation.

The required guarantee allows squared Frobenius error at most 1 + epsilon times the optimal error. An existing deterministic method achieves this using O(dk/epsilon) words of memory, where d is the number of columns. The authors ask whether a streaming algorithm could use substantially less space while retaining that guarantee.

They prove a lower bound of Ω(dk/epsilon) bits, even for randomized algorithms that only need to succeed with constant probability. This nearly matches the existing upper bound, with the remaining distinction being bits versus machine words. The result strengthens the earlier Ω(dk) bound by showing that the dependence on the requested approximation accuracy also imposes a fundamental memory cost.
neurips-2014-low-rank-approximation-lowe.tldr: A streaming lower bound nearly matches known memory requirements for relative-error low-rank approximation, even with randomization.

paragraphs: Random forests combine randomized decision trees and are attractive for efficient prediction. Popular variants train on batches of data, while online settings require updating a model as observations arrive. The paper identifies a drawback of existing online forests: they can need more training data than batch counterparts to reach comparable predictive performance.

The authors construct Mondrian forests using Mondrian processes. These forests can grow incrementally, and their online construction produces the same distribution over forests as their batch construction. This is a distributional equivalence between the two training procedures; it connects incremental updates to a corresponding batch model in a precise way.

The reported experiments find predictive performance comparable to existing online random forests and periodically retrained batch forests, alongside speed gains exceeding an order of magnitude. The resulting advantage is a better measured balance between computation and accuracy. The paper therefore combines an online tree-building construction with both a theoretical link to batch training and empirical evidence of efficient prediction learning as data arrive.
neurips-2014-mondrian-forests-efficient-.tldr: Mondrian forests match their batch construction in distribution while delivering competitive online accuracy and reported speed gains exceeding tenfold.

paragraphs: Multilabel prediction involves choosing several labels whose relationships can matter to the result. Conditional Markov networks represent such structured outputs with a score function. This paper investigates how a collection of spanning trees can represent that score and provide a more manageable basis for learning.

The authors show that the usual network score can be written as an expectation over scores associated with its spanning trees. They further show that a small random sample of output trees can retain a significant fraction of the margin achieved by the complete graph. The margin result explains why sampling relatively few trees can still preserve a meaningful part of the full model's separation.

The paper also gives conditions under which inference is tractable. That qualification matters: computational tractability is established under those conditions, rather than for every possible structured prediction problem. Experiments confirm that the approach supports practical learning on realistic datasets. Together, the score decomposition, margin result, and inference conditions provide a basis for scalable learning through sampled tree structures.
neurips-2014-multilabel-structured-outpu.tldr: Randomly sampled spanning trees can retain a significant fraction of a full structured model's margin and support tractable inference under stated conditions.

paragraphs: Distributed learning can split training examples among workers or split the model's parameters among them. This paper focuses on the second approach, model parallelism, in which workers concurrently update different parameters. The authors argue that dependencies among these updates create distinct challenges for systems, algorithms, and correctness analysis.

They introduce STRADS, a system with a programming abstraction for scheduling parameter updates. Its scheduling uses structural properties of the learning program that can change during execution. The abstraction lets implementations balance scheduling efficiency against how faithfully they respect the model's intrinsic dependencies, while also improving memory efficiency in distributed learning.

The paper demonstrates model-parallel algorithms on topic modeling, matrix factorization, and Lasso, comparing STRADS implementations with popular alternatives. These demonstrations support the system's usefulness across several learning problems. The main contribution is to make parameter-update scheduling an explicit part of distributed execution, so decisions about concurrent work can respond to the structure of the model being trained rather than relying only on a division of the input data.
neurips-2014-on-model-parallelization-an.tldr: STRADS schedules distributed parameter updates using changing model structure to balance efficiency, dependencies, and memory use.

paragraphs: Multitask feature learning seeks useful representations across related prediction tasks. This paper studies a framework that expresses each task's model parameters as the product of a shared component and a task-specific component. Several earlier methods fit within this formulation, making it a common basis for examining how sharing and individual task behavior interact.

The authors analyze different regularization choices for the two components. They prove an equivalence with approaches that jointly regularize all task parameters, while allowing a more general family of regularizers. They also derive an analytical relationship between the shared and task-specific components, clarifying how regularization shrinks parameters within the multiplicative representation.

The analysis motivates two new learning formulations obtained by varying the framework's parameters. Empirical comparisons with state-of-the-art methods reveal relative advantages of these formulations. The paper's contribution is therefore both explanatory and constructive: it connects existing approaches through a mathematical framework and uses that connection to develop further choices for learning features across multiple tasks.
neurips-2014-on-multiplicative-multitask.tldr: A multiplicative framework connects shared and task-specific feature learning to joint regularization and motivates two new formulations.

paragraphs: Matrix completion reconstructs information about a matrix from only some of its entries. This paper considers observations drawn from a finite set of possible values, such as recommendation ratings or class labels. That setting calls for a probabilistic treatment of discrete observations rather than focusing only on directly observed real-valued entries.

The authors study an estimator with nuclear norm regularization, which encourages low-rank structure. Their sampling setup permits entries to be observed nonuniformly, accommodating unequal sampling probabilities across the matrix. The theoretical analysis bounds the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the true and estimated distributions, measuring accuracy in terms of how well the estimated probabilities match the underlying ones.

The paper also proposes an efficient algorithm based on lifted coordinate gradient descent for potentially high-dimensional problems. This pairs a statistical analysis with a practical optimization approach. The overall contribution extends low-rank matrix completion to finite-valued observations and a broader sampling scheme, while grounding its recovery guarantees in distributional accuracy.
neurips-2014-probabilistic-low-rank-matr.tldr: Finite-valued matrix completion receives distributional error bounds under nonuniform sampling and an efficient optimization algorithm.

paragraphs: Submodular function minimization appears in learning and vision, but algorithms with strong general polynomial-time guarantees can be impractical. The Fujishige-Wolfe approach has strong reported empirical performance, yet its theoretical behavior was poorly understood. It solves a geometric problem involving the point of minimum Euclidean norm in a polytope.

The authors prove that after t iterations, Wolfe's algorithm obtains an O(1/t)-approximate solution to this minimum-norm problem. They also establish a robust version of the theorem linking that geometric problem to submodular minimization: an O(1/n²)-accurate minimum-norm solution suffices to obtain an exact submodular minimum. This connects approximate geometric progress to exact discrete optimization.

Combining these results gives a pseudo-polynomial runtime guarantee for the Fujishige-Wolfe method. The stated bound is O(n⁷F²), where F bounds the largest change in function value caused by one element. Its dependence on F is part of the guarantee. The contribution supplies a convergence explanation for a practically successful method and a quantitative route from its iterations to an exact solution.
neurips-2014-provable-submodular-minimiz.tldr: Convergence and robustness results give the Fujishige-Wolfe submodular minimization algorithm a pseudo-polynomial runtime guarantee.

paragraphs: Probabilistic graphical models specify joint distributions through relationships among variables. This paper develops a framework for applying sequential Monte Carlo to inference in these models. The central challenge is to turn a distribution described by a graph into a sequence of targets that a sequential sampling method can follow.

The authors construct a sequential decomposition of the graphical model. It produces auxiliary distributions on probability spaces that grow as the sequence progresses. Sequential Monte Carlo targets these intermediate distributions, ultimately approximating the model's full joint distribution. This provides a systematic connection between the graph's probabilistic description and a sequential inference procedure.

A key property is an unbiased estimate of the partition function, the normalizing quantity associated with the model. Unbiasedness refers to the estimator's average, rather than making each estimate exact. The authors also show how to embed the sampler in particle Markov chain Monte Carlo to construct algorithms that sample high-dimensional blocks. The framework therefore supports both joint-distribution approximation and a building block for broader sampling methods.
neurips-2014-sequential-monte-carlo-for-.tldr: Sequential decompositions enable SMC inference in graphical models, unbiased partition-function estimation, and particle MCMC block sampling.

paragraphs: The Indian Buffet Process is a statistical tool for modeling distributions over binary matrices. Inference can be computationally expensive when performed through variational Bayes or sampling. This paper develops a spectral alternative intended to make inference more efficient while providing mathematical guarantees about its behavior.

The foundation is a new tensor-based characterization of the process's moments, together with corresponding characterizations for two applications. Moments summarize aspects of a distribution; arranging their relationships in tensor form supplies the structure used by the proposed inference method. The authors turn this characterization into an efficient iterative algorithm and establish concentration bounds and reconstruction guarantees.

On several reference problems, the algorithm achieves better accuracy with less computation than a comparable variational Bayesian approach. These are comparative findings on the evaluated problems, accompanying the theoretical results. The contribution links a new mathematical description of the Indian Buffet Process to an inference procedure, showing how moment structure can support both computational improvements and formal analysis.
neurips-2014-spectral-methods-for-indian.tldr: A tensor-moment characterization enables efficient spectral Indian Buffet Process inference with guarantees and favorable reported accuracy and computation.

paragraphs: Bipartite ranking learns scores that place positive examples ahead of negative ones. In many ranking tasks, accuracy near the top of the list is especially important. This paper addresses the computational expense of optimizing that region, where existing approaches often require more than linear growth in work as training data increase.

The authors propose TopPush, an approach aimed directly at accuracy among the highest-ranked instances. Its computational complexity is linear in the number of training instances. This scaling matters because it makes the size of the training set a more manageable contributor to computational cost while retaining the focus on the top of the ranking.

The paper also derives a generalization error bound specifically for top-ranked instances, connecting its training approach to performance beyond the training examples. Empirically, TopPush is highly competitive with state-of-the-art approaches and runs 10–100 times faster in the reported study. The contribution combines an efficient ranking objective and algorithm with theoretical analysis targeted to the same part of the list that motivates the method.
neurips-2014-top-rank-optimization-in-li.tldr: TopPush optimizes top-of-list ranking accuracy with linear training-set complexity and reported speed gains of 10–100 times.

paragraphs: Off-policy reinforcement learning uses experience collected under one policy to learn about another. Importance sampling helps account for this difference, but its weighted variant has been difficult to incorporate into function approximation. This paper develops a way to bring its benefits into learning with linear approximations.

The first step is to interpret weighted importance sampling as a special case of assigning weights to individual training-sample errors. This reframing connects the sampling correction to the objective used for learning from data. The authors show theoretical and empirical benefits from this error-weighting perspective that resemble those of weighted importance sampling itself.

The second step applies the idea to off-policy LSTD(lambda), producing WIS-LSTD(lambda). Empirical results show that the new algorithm can converge much faster and more reliably than conventional off-policy LSTD(lambda). The claim is a demonstrated possibility rather than a universal ordering across all problems. Together, the reformulation and algorithm provide a concrete route for using weighted importance sampling ideas when value estimates are represented by a linear function approximator.
neurips-2014-weighted-importance-samplin.tldr: Recasting weighted importance sampling as sample-error weighting yields an off-policy LSTD variant with potentially faster, more reliable convergence.
